title: Britain's Most Haunted: 15 Places and the Ghost Slang to Go With Them
excerpt: 15 of Britain's most haunted places you can actually visit, from the Tower of London to Glamis Castle, paired with British ghost slang: bogles, boggarts, wraiths and more.
content:
Part of our British Slang & Lingo series. Jump to more slang ↓

Britain does ghosts better than anywhere else. Put a thousand years of executions, plagues, battles and family feuds into a small island full of damp castles and creaking inns, and you get a country where seemingly every old building has a Grey Lady, a phantom monk or a headless queen.

The British also have a wonderfully rich vocabulary for things that go bump in the night. Americans have ghosts and the boogeyman. The British have bogles, boggarts, barghests, wraiths and fetches, not to mention the collywobbles.

So here are 15 of Britain’s most famously haunted places, all of which you can visit, each paired with a piece of British ghost slang to take with you. A word of caution: these are legends. Some have real history behind them, some have been embroidered over the centuries, and a few were simply made up. We’ve pointed out which is which where we can. (For more spooky spots, see our earlier list of the most allegedly haunted places in Britain.)

1. The Tower of London

If any building in Britain should be haunted, it’s this one. Anne Boleyn, Henry VIII’s second wife, was beheaded at the Tower on May 19, 1536, and buried in the Chapel of St Peter ad Vincula. According to Historic Royal Palaces, which runs the Tower, her ghost has been seen leading a procession from Tower Green to the chapel.

She has plenty of company. Margaret Pole, Countess of Salisbury, was executed on Tower Green in 1541 at the age of 67 by a blundering executioner, and her screams are said to echo there still. The Princes in the Tower, the boy king Edward V and his brother Richard, are said to walk hand in hand. And in 1864 a soldier found collapsed on duty outside the King’s House claimed a white figure had come at him, and that his bayonet went straight through it. He was acquitted after witnesses backed up his story.

The slang: “give up the ghost.” To die, or, these days, for a machine to stop working (“the car finally gave up the ghost”). The phrase goes all the way back to Old English, when “ghost” meant the soul or spirit. Its cousin, “not a ghost of a chance,” uses “ghost” in the old sense of a faint shadow of something.

Visiting: Open year-round. Book ahead at hrp.org.uk.

2. Hampton Court Palace, Surrey

Henry VIII’s fifth wife, Catherine Howard, was arrested at Hampton Court and beheaded in 1542. Legend says she broke free from her guards and ran screaming down a corridor towards the Chapel, where Henry was at prayer, before being dragged away. It’s now known as the Haunted Gallery.

Then there’s Sybil Penn, who nursed the young Elizabeth I through smallpox in 1562, caught it herself and died. When her tomb was disturbed in 1829, sightings of a “Grey Lady” began, along with the whirr of a spinning wheel. Most famously, in October 2003 the palace’s CCTV caught a fire door flying open on three days in a row, and on the second day a robed figure appeared in the doorway. As Historic Royal Palaces puts it: “No living soul has ever come forward to admit that this was their prank.”

The slang: “the collywobbles.” A nervous, fluttery feeling of fear, or an upset stomach, which is often the same thing. It’s a British word, first recorded in 1823, probably from “colic” and “wobble.” Exactly what you’d feel walking down the Haunted Gallery after dark.

Visiting: Open year-round. Adult tickets from £27.20 (about $36.45). The palace runs a Halloween program in late October.

3. Theatre Royal Drury Lane, London

Every West End theater claims a ghost, but Drury Lane’s is the most famous. The Man in Grey wears an 18th-century cloak and tricorn hat, and is said to appear during daytime performances, cross the upper circle and vanish into a wall. According to the theater’s owners, workmen found a skeleton bricked into that very wall during an 1842 refurbishment, with scraps of grey cloth and a knife between its ribs. That story rests on theater lore rather than any record we could find.

Actors consider him good luck: he’s supposed to appear before a long-running hit. Whole casts claim to have seen him at curtain calls, during The Dancing Years in 1939 and Miss Saigon in 1999.

The slang: “put the wind up someone.” To frighten or alarm someone. If you’re the one who’s scared, you’ve “got the wind up.” It’s British and informal: “Seeing that figure in the upper circle really put the wind up me.”

Visiting: Backstage tours of the theater run Wednesday to Saturday, from about £23 ($30.80).

4. Highgate Cemetery, London

With its ivy-choked Victorian tombs and the Egyptian Avenue, Highgate is spooky enough without a monster. But in 1970 it got one. It began when a young man named David Farrant wrote to the local newspaper about a “grey figure” he’d seen there on Christmas Eve 1969. Another man, Sean Manchester, turned the story into a vampire hunt, and on Friday, March 13, 1970, after television interviews, a crowd of around 100 people broke into the cemetery to find it.

Farrant was later arrested in the cemetery with a stake and crucifix, and eventually jailed in 1974 for damaging memorials. Farrant himself never claimed to have seen a vampire, and the two men feuded for decades. It was, frankly, more media circus than haunting, but the “Highgate Vampire” has never quite gone away.

The slang: “give someone the creeps.” To make someone feel nervous and slightly frightened. “The creeps,” meaning a feeling of dread, dates to 1849, and fittingly it’s first found in the work of that great Londoner Charles Dickens.

Visiting: Open daily (10am–4pm in winter). Both the East and West cemeteries can now be explored on your own, though guided tours are recommended. Book at highgatecemetery.org.

5. Pluckley, Kent

This pretty Kent village is famous as “the most haunted village in England,” said to be home to a dozen ghosts: a Red Lady and a White Lady at the church, a highwayman at Fright Corner, a screaming man at the old brickworks, a Watercress Woman, a phantom coach and horses and a monk.

You’ll often read that it holds a Guinness World Record. It doesn’t, quite. The village appeared in the 1989 Guinness Book of Records with “at least twelve” ghosts, but Guinness doesn’t recognize it as a current record. And research published in 2025 by Dr. Simon Moreton of the University of the West of England found that several of the ghosts trace back to real local deaths, while others, including the phantom coach and the monk, were invented for a 1962 magazine article. It’s still a lovely, atmospheric place, but if you go, remember that it’s people’s home and be respectful.

The slang: “ghoulies and ghosties and long-leggedy beasties, and things that go bump in the night.” This much-loved rhyme is often described as an ancient Cornish or Scottish prayer. In fact, the earliest version anyone has found was printed in Edinburgh in 1905, described as being “from a quaint old Litany.” Old-sounding, then, but not that old.

6. Blickling Estate, Norfolk

Anne Boleyn gets around. Blickling, now cared for by the National Trust, is thought to be where she was born, and the Trust says she “reappears every year on 19 May, the anniversary of her execution.” In the most popular version of the story, she arrives at dusk in a coach driven by a headless horseman, holding her own head in her lap.

A spoilsport footnote: the grand red-brick hall you see today was built in the 1600s, long after Anne’s death, so she’d have trouble recognizing it.

The slang: “Black Shuck.” Norfolk has its own ghost, and it’s a dog. Black Shuck is a huge, shaggy black hound with glowing eyes said to roam the lanes and coast of East Anglia. “Shuck” is thought to come from the Old English scucca, meaning devil or fiend. On August 4, 1577, during a violent storm, a black dog was said to have burst into churches at Bungay and Blythburgh in Suffolk, killing worshippers, and a pamphlet published that year told the tale.

Visiting: Open year-round. Adult admission £18 (about $24.10).

7. Berry Pomeroy Castle, Devon

Hidden in deep woods near Totnes, Berry Pomeroy is a strange place: a medieval castle with the shell of a grand Elizabethan mansion inside it, begun by the Seymour family around 1560, never finished and abandoned by 1700. English Heritage, which looks after it, says the ruins “inspired blood-curdling ghost stories.”

The two most famous are the White Lady, said to be Margaret Pomeroy, imprisoned in the dungeons by a sister jealous of her beauty, and the Blue Lady, a tragic figure who lures men to their deaths and whose appearance was said to foretell a death in the family.

The slang: “the White Lady.” Britain is full of White Ladies and Grey Ladies, female ghosts usually linked to a tragic death, a lost love or an imprisonment. Wales has its own version, Y Ladi Wen, which Amgueddfa Cymru – Museum Wales calls one of the two most common ghosts in Welsh folklore.

Visiting: Check english-heritage.org.uk for current opening days, which change with the season. An audio guide tells the ghost stories.

8. Jamaica Inn, Cornwall

Standing alone on the windswept heights of Bodmin Moor, Jamaica Inn has the perfect setting for a ghost story. Daphne du Maurier certainly thought so: she got lost riding on the moor in November 1930 and spent the night here, and the experience inspired her 1936 novel Jamaica Inn, about a gang of smugglers and wreckers.

The inn claims several ghosts, including a man said to have been murdered after leaving his drink unfinished in the bar, who has been seen sitting on the wall outside, and a figure in a tricorn hat in one of the bedrooms. There’s no record of the murder, but it’s a wonderfully moody spot for a pint. Jamaica Inn is still a working inn, with a smugglers’ museum and a room devoted to du Maurier, including her writing desk. It hosts regular paranormal investigation nights.

The slang: “knockers.” In Cornish and Devon folklore, knockers were spirits who lived in the tin mines, tapping on the rock to lead miners to rich seams or warn them of a cave-in. When Cornish miners emigrated to America in the 19th century, the knockers came too, and became the “tommyknockers” of the mining towns of the American West.

9. Caerphilly Castle, Wales

Caerphilly, near Cardiff, is the largest castle in Wales and one of the most impressive in Britain, ringed by artificial lakes and famous for its leaning tower. It has also just reopened after two years of conservation work by Cadw, the Welsh government’s historic environment service.

It also has one of Welsh folklore’s most terrifying creatures. Amgueddfa Cymru – Museum Wales tells of the Gwrach-y-Rhibyn, a hag-spirit said to fly around the castle moat “screeching out the names of those about to die,” with long black hair, long black teeth, sunken eyes and bat-like wings.

The slang: “corpse candle” (cannwyll corff). In Welsh folklore, a corpse candle is a mysterious light seen moving along the road at night, foretelling a death or a funeral. The National Library of Wales has collected accounts of them from Ceredigion and Carmarthenshire.

Visiting: Open daily (10am–4pm in winter). Adult admission £12.90 (about $17.30). Some areas may be closed while redevelopment work continues.

10. Treasurer’s House, York

York claims to be the most haunted city in Europe, and its most famous ghost story happened in the cellar of this elegant house near York Minster. In February 1953, a young apprentice heating engineer named Harry Martindale was working down there when he heard a horn. Then, he said, a troop of around 20 Roman soldiers came through the wall, one of them on horseback.

The detail that made his story famous: he could only see them from the knees up, as if they were walking on a lower surface. A Roman road lies buried about 18 inches below the cellar floor. Martindale, who died in 2014, stuck to his story for the rest of his life, although, as the National Trust admits, many academics dismissed it.

The slang: “barghest.” In Yorkshire folklore, a barghest is a ghost or goblin that often takes the form of a huge black dog, and whose appearance means misfortune. The word may come from dialect “bargh” (a hill or ridge) and “ghest” (ghost).

Visiting: The National Trust runs guided tours from spring to fall and self-guided visits in winter. Check opening days before you go.

11. Pendle Hill, Lancashire

This brooding hill isn’t haunted by a single ghost so much as by one of the darkest episodes in English history. In 1612, a dozen people from the villages around Pendle were accused of witchcraft. Elizabeth Southerns, known as “Old Demdike,” died in jail before trial. After trials at Lancaster and York, ten were hanged, including Anne Whittle (“Old Chattox”) and Alice Nutter, a woman of some standing. The star witness against her own family was nine-year-old Jennet Device.

The story has made Pendle a magnet at Halloween, when people traditionally climb the hill at night. It’s not an organized event, and in some years police have asked people to stay away, so check local advice if you’re tempted.

The slang: “boggart.” A Lancashire and Yorkshire word for a mischievous or malevolent spirit, usually one that haunts a particular place: a lane, a field, a house. It dates back to at least the 1560s. Manchester even has a park called Boggart Hole Clough. Harry Potter fans will recognize the word, but it was haunting northern England for four centuries before J.K. Rowling borrowed it.

12. Chillingham Castle, Northumberland

Chillingham, near the Scottish border, is regularly called one of the most haunted castles in Britain, and it leans into that reputation with gusto. Its most famous ghost is the “Blue Boy” or “Radiant Boy,” a glowing figure said to have haunted the Pink Room. The castle’s own ghost list also includes a ghost in the White Pantry and voices in the chapel. The castle has been restored by the Wakefield family since 1982, and its torture chamber is not for the squeamish.

The slang: “gytrash.” A northern English spirit that takes the form of an animal. The word is best known from Charlotte Brontë’s Jane Eyre (1847), in which Jane recalls “a North-of-England spirit called a ‘Gytrash,’ which, in the form of horse, mule, or large dog, haunted solitary ways, and sometimes came upon belated travellers.” (If you’re visiting the North East, brush up on your Geordie slang too.)

Visiting: Open spring to fall, then closed for the season. Adult admission £15 (about $20.10). Evening ghost tours (£25, about $33.50) continue on selected dates into December and sell out fast.

13. Muncaster Castle, Cumbria

On the edge of the Lake District, Muncaster is haunted by a jester. Tom Skelton, “Tom Fool,” was jester to the Pennington family, and the castle says he was a menace: he would send travelers he disliked off towards the deadly quicksands. His portrait still hangs at Muncaster. The castle’s Tapestry Room is said to be its most haunted, with footsteps, a door handle that turns by itself and the sound of a child crying. You can even book an overnight “Ghost Sit” there.

The slang: “tomfoolery” (myth busted). You’ll often hear that Tom Skelton gave us the word “tomfoolery.” Sadly, no. “Tom Fool” was already in use as a name for a fool in the 1300s, long before Skelton was born. “Tomfoolery” itself appears around 1800.

Visiting: The main season runs spring to late October, with winter weekend openings. Adult admission to the castle and gardens is £24.95 (about $33.45) in the main season and £19.50 (about $26.15) in winter.

14. The Real Mary King’s Close, Edinburgh

Beneath the Royal Mile lies a buried street. Mary King’s Close, named after a 17th-century merchant, was partly demolished and built over when the Royal Exchange (now the City Chambers) went up in 1753. Today you can walk its dark, narrow passages on a guided tour.

Its most famous resident is “Annie.” In 1992 a Japanese psychic, Aiko Gibo, visiting the close said she sensed a little girl who had been abandoned there, dying of plague, and had lost her doll. Gibo left a doll for her, and visitors have been leaving toys in “Annie’s Room” ever since. Money left there has raised thousands for Edinburgh’s children’s hospital. To its credit, the attraction itself points out that no child called Annie appears in the historical records.

The slang: “bogle.” A Scots word for a ghost, goblin or terrifying spirit, in use since around 1500 and popularized by Robert Burns and Sir Walter Scott. While you’re in Scotland, you might also hear a ghost called a ghaist, as in Burns’s line “Whare ghaists and houlets nightly cry” (houlets are owls).

Visiting: Open daily. Tours from £25 (about $33.50); book ahead.

15. Glamis Castle, Angus

The childhood home of the late Queen Mother, and the birthplace of Princess Margaret in 1930, Glamis looks like a fairy-tale castle. Its legends are anything but. The most famous is the “Monster of Glamis”: a deformed heir supposedly hidden away in a secret room that was later bricked up. Guests are said to have hung towels from every window to find which room didn’t have one.

There’s also the ghost of Janet Douglas, Lady Glamis, burned at the stake in Edinburgh in 1537 on charges of witchcraft and plotting to poison the King. She’s said to haunt the chapel, where a seat is kept free for her. Then there’s “Earl Beardie,” a 15th-century lord who played cards with the Devil on the Sabbath and lost his soul. (Shakespeare made Macbeth “Thane of Glamis,” but the real Macbeth had no known link to the castle.)

The slang: “wraith.” A ghost, especially the exact likeness of a living person, seen just before or after their death. It’s a Scottish word, of uncertain origin, first recorded in the 1510s. A similar word from English and Irish dialect is a “fetch”: a person’s ghostly double, whose appearance foretells their death.

Visiting: Glamis closes for winter just before Christmas and reopens in spring. Castle tours cost £19.50 (about $26.15). Check glamis-castle.co.uk for dates.

More British Ghost Slang

  • Bogeyman: The British spelling. “Boogeyman” is the American version, which only appears in the 20th century.
  • Hobgoblin: A mischievous sprite, from “hob” (a pet form of Robin, as in Robin Goodfellow) and “goblin.” In use since the 1520s.
  • Frit: Northern and Midlands dialect for “frightened.” Margaret Thatcher, who grew up in Lincolnshire, famously used it in the House of Commons in 1983 to taunt an opponent: “Afraid? Frightened? Frit?”
  • Will-o’-the-wisp: A ghostly light over marshes that leads travelers astray. It used to be called a “jack-o’-lantern” too. Using that name for a carved pumpkin is an American invention of the 1800s.
  • Guising: The Scottish Halloween tradition of going door to door in disguise. The word goes back to at least the 1860s, and it’s a cousin of American trick-or-treating.
  • Mischief Night: A night of pranks in northern England. In most of Yorkshire it’s now November 4, the night before Bonfire Night, and around Liverpool, October 30.
  • Nos Calan Gaeaf: The Welsh name for Halloween night, the eve of the first day of winter. Children in North Wales were told to run home when the bonfires died down, or the Hwch Ddu Gwta, a tailless black sow, would catch the last one.
